item.title: New Plugin Release 4.2.0
item.description: Released version 4.2.0 - an important security release with JWT audience checks, session revocation on password change, and many fixes
item.content:encoded:
The version 4.2.0 has been released today on WordPress.

Upgrade notice

Important security release. It fixes multiple security vulnerabilities affecting authentication, authorization, and REST API endpoints. All users are strongly encouraged to upgrade as soon as possible. Review the Breaking Changes section before upgrading.

Security​

  • Fixed multiple security vulnerabilities affecting authentication, authorization, and REST API endpoints
  • Strengthened validation and authorization across the affected endpoints
  • Improved the data returned by REST API endpoints
  • Added security regression tests to prevent these issues from coming back

New Features​

  • Expected audience (aud) - new optional setting for the plugin's own JWTs (Authentication) and for each JWT Rule. When set, new JWTs carry that aud and only JWTs whose aud contains it are accepted (new error code 130). Read more about the audience setting.
  • Revoke sessions on password change - new option in Authentication, off by default. When on, changing a password deletes the user's refresh tokens and rejects every JWT issued before the change. JWTs without an iat claim are then also rejected for that user. Read more about revoking sessions.
  • /auth now checks the password with wp_authenticate(), so brute-force and user-block plugins (Limit Login Attempts, Wordfence and similar) protect it like wp-login.php. Application passwords can't be exchanged for a JWT. Read more about password checks.
  • OAuth backward-compatibility options - new options, off by default, to accept tokens that aren't bound to the configured app. They are Allow tokens issued for other Google clients, Allow tokens issued for other Facebook apps, Allow tokens issued for other GitHub apps (also accepts personal access tokens) and Auth0 Allow opaque access tokens. The admin screen shows a security warning while one is on, because any app on that provider could then log its users into the matching WordPress accounts. See OAuth backward compatibility.
  • Dashboard security notices - a new Security notices section lists the enabled options and settings that weaken security (the critical and warning findings of the security report), most severe first. Click a notice to open the matching settings tab. The dashboard and the AI security-report ability also report the OAuth options above when they are on. See the Dashboard.
  • The AI Abilities security report now warns when authentication with password_hash is enabled
  • Admin: optional support banner with a donation link at the top of the settings page. It can be dismissed for 6 months, and no features are locked behind donations

Breaking Changes​

Why these changes are breaking

These changes were introduced on purpose to strengthen the security of your WordPress site, so most of them can't be kept optional. The OAuth token checks are the exception. The new options Allow tokens issued for other Google clients, Allow opaque access tokens, Allow tokens issued for other Facebook apps, and Allow tokens issued for other GitHub apps turn them off for one provider each. When one is on, your applications stay backward compatible and keep working as before 4.2.0, but without the security fix for that provider. See OAuth backward compatibility.

  • WordPress 6.2 or newer is required (was 4.4). The plugin's database queries use the %i identifier placeholder added in WordPress 6.2.

  • OAuth login links - the OAuth login buttons (Google, Auth0, Facebook, GitHub) now go through the plugin, which redirects to the provider. Custom login buttons or links that send visitors straight to the provider with the plugin's callback as redirect_uri stop working. Link to GET /oauth/token?provider=<provider> instead. See the OAuth flow.

  • OAuth tokens - tokens sent to the OAuth endpoint (and Google id_tokens used on all endpoints) must be issued for the app configured in the plugin:

    • a Facebook or GitHub access_token must belong to the configured app (GitHub personal access tokens are rejected)
    • a Google id_token must have the configured Client ID as aud
    • an Auth0 access_token must be a JWT issued for the configured Auth0 Client ID (azp or aud), so opaque Auth0 access tokens are rejected

    To stay backward compatible, turn on the matching new OAuth option. See OAuth backward compatibility.

  • Reset password - POST /user/reset_password with an unknown email now answers 200 instead of 404 with the "Wrong user." message.

  • Reverse proxy - with "Trust reverse proxy IP headers" on, the client IP is read from the last X-Forwarded-For entry only. Sites whose proxy sends the client IP only in Client-IP must switch the proxy to X-Forwarded-For. See Trust reverse proxy IP headers.

  • Two-factor - after too many wrong two-factor codes (30 by default, Two Factor filter two_factor_failed_attempt_limit) sent to POST /auth/2fa or the OAuth two-factor form, the user's password is reset and the user and admin are emailed, as on wp-login.php. Read more about two-factor failed codes.

  • API keys on /batch/v1 - API keys need the create, update and delete permissions, otherwise they get 401. See API Keys.

  • HTTP status of error responses - client errors that used to answer 500 now answer their real status (401, 403, 404, 422 or 429). The error_code values didn't change, so code that checks error_code keeps working. See the full list of changed statuses.

  • Audience - once you set an expected audience, JWTs issued before it have no aud and stop working, so users must log in again

Bug Fixes​

  • Fix the Facebook browser login returning a 500 error instead of the login page with the error message when Facebook rejects the code
  • Fix two parallel /auth/refresh calls with the same refresh token both getting a new JWT: a refresh token can now be used once only
  • Fix API keys and refresh tokens staying in the database when a user is deleted in wp-admin, and an API key of a deleted user causing a 500 error instead of 401
  • Fix /auth rejecting Base64 passwords that contain ', " or \. Invalid Base64 now answers "Wrong user credentials."
  • Fix /auth and /auth/refresh returning a refresh token that couldn't be saved: they now answer 500 (new error code 131)
  • Fix API key expires_at accepting any text: it must be a date, a date time or an ISO 8601 date (new error code 132), is read as UTC and stored as UTC. The admin form now sends the browser's local time converted to UTC
  • Fix the Delete button in Security > Revoked Tokens, which always failed with "Invalid revoked token ID."
  • Failing to store the two-factor session now has its own error code 133 (500). It used to share code 107 with "two-factor session expired"

API Reference​

  • Every endpoint in the API reference now documents its real request parameters, status codes and error codes, with examples taken from the plugin messages
  • The endpoints used by the plugin admin screens (/api-keys* and /revoked-tokens*) are tagged internal, with their access rules: revoked tokens are for administrators only, and API keys can be managed by their owner, while administrators can manage every user's keys

If you encounter any issues after updating, please open an issue on GitHub.

item.title: New Plugin Release 4.1.1
item.description: Released version 4.1.1 - a security release with stricter CORS origin rules for JWTs and a fix for JWT from session
item.content:encoded:
The version 4.1.1 has been released today on WordPress.

A security release. Updating is recommended for everyone. If a browser app on another origin sends the JWT, list that origin in the CORS Allow origin setting before updating.

Security​

  • Fixed a security vulnerability affecting JWT authentication of REST requests (reported via Patchstack)

Breaking Changes​

  • Cross-origin browser apps that send the JWT must have their origin listed in the CORS Allow origin setting. A * entry trusts the Authorization header only - cookie and session JWTs are never trusted
  • With CORS disabled (or Allow origin off), a JWT sent by a browser page on another site, even in the Authorization header, is ignored

Requests from the site itself, server-to-server calls, mobile apps and JWTs passed in the URL (for example, autologin links) are not affected.

Read more about cross-site requests and CORS.

Bug Fixes​

  • Fix "JWT from session" making every plugin endpoint and Protect Endpoints fail with a 500 error (call to an undefined session function)

If you encounter any issues after updating, please open an issue on GitHub.

item.title: New Plugin Release 4.1.0
item.description: Released version 4.1.0 - AI Abilities (MCP) integration, security hardening, faster API key and WooCommerce requests, and CORS fixes
item.content:encoded:
The version 4.1.0 has been released today on WordPress.

This release adds the AI Abilities (MCP) integration, hardens security across Protect Endpoints, registration, webhooks and integrations, cuts database work on every authenticated request and fixes CORS headers on error responses. Updating is recommended for everyone.

New Features​

  • AI Abilities (MCP) - let AI agents manage and troubleshoot the plugin through the WordPress Abilities API (WordPress 6.9+). Read more about the AI Abilities integration.
  • CORS: multiple allowed origins - Access-Control-Allow-Origin now accepts a comma-separated list. The matching request origin is echoed back, and * echoes the request origin so credentialed requests work (#179). Read more about CORS.
  • New API Keys setting - Update "Last used" - choose whether a key's "Last used" time is saved at most once per minute (the new default) or on every request. Read more about API Keys.

Security​

  • Fix CSRF in the Force Login integration on cookie-authenticated REST requests (reported via Patchstack)
  • The JWT middleware and the WooCommerce integration now check the resolved REST route instead of searching the URL
  • Protect Endpoints now enforces JWT + Roles rules for logged-in (cookie-authenticated) users and API key owners. Read more about Protect Endpoints.
  • Registration never sets capability, user level or session meta keys from the request, even when they are listed in Allowed User Meta Keys
  • Webhook calls time out after at most 30 seconds (0 now means 30 seconds instead of no timeout), so a slow webhook endpoint can't hang logins
  • Secrets (auth codes, JWT rule keys, webhook header values) are no longer written in plain text to the Settings Saved audit log entry

Performance​

  • Login no longer creates two WordPress sessions instead of one (autologin, register with auto-login, OAuth), reducing database writes per login
  • The API key "last used" timestamp is updated at most once per minute per key by default, instead of on every request
  • Remove an extra database query on every API key request
  • WooCommerce integration: JWT requests are authenticated without a full login, so API calls no longer create a new WordPress session, set auth cookies or fire wp_login on every request
  • Load the WordPress admin user functions only when deleting a user, instead of on every request
  • Protect Endpoints no longer checks the revoked-token table twice for every JWT-authenticated request, and checks access once per REST request instead of every time WordPress reads the route list
  • The Force Login, WooCommerce and WPGraphQL integrations reuse the plugin settings instead of re-reading and decoding them on every REST request

Bug Fixes​

  • Fix CORS headers missing on REST error responses (401/403 from JWT authentication and protected endpoints) (#179)

If you encounter any issues after updating, please open an issue on GitHub.

item.title: New Plugin Release 4.0.0
item.description: Released version 4.0.0 - major redesign, new features, OAuth expansion, 2FA, API Keys, Audit Logs, Webhooks, and more
item.content:encoded:
The version 4.0.0 has been released today on WordPress.

This is a major release packed with new features, a redesigned admin interface, expanded OAuth provider support, and important security and usability improvements. Please read the breaking changes section carefully before upgrading.

New Features​

Redesigned Admin Interface​

The plugin settings interface has been redesigned to provide a cleaner, more modern, and intuitive user experience. Settings are now better organized, easier to discover, and simpler to configure, reducing the need to consult documentation for common setup tasks. The refreshed layout improves navigation and helps users configure JWT authentication more efficiently.

The new admin UI also includes full Light and Dark Mode support, automatically adapting to your preferred WordPress admin theme for a consistent and comfortable experience.

Behind the scenes, all frontend assets (CSS, JavaScript, and images) have been reorganized into a dedicated assets/ directory, resulting in a cleaner, more maintainable plugin structure, and improved developer experience.

Audit Logs​

A new Audit Logs section gives you visibility into authentication events across your WordPress site. You can now track login attempts, token refreshes, user registrations, password resets, and more - all with timestamps and relevant metadata. Audit log entries are stored in a dedicated database table and can be browsed directly from the plugin settings.

Webhooks​

Outbound webhooks are now supported. You can configure HTTP callbacks that fire on key plugin events - such as user login, registration, authentication, and more. Each webhook call result is optionally logged, giving you a full audit trail of outbound notifications.

API Keys (X-API-Key)​

A new API Keys management system lets you create and manage X-API-Key tokens that grant authenticated access to WordPress REST endpoints. This is useful for machine-to-machine integrations where you need stable, long-lived credentials without issuing JWTs.

Key features include:

  • Full CRUD interface for managing keys (create, update, list, delete, revoke)
  • Configurable permissions per key
  • JWT authentication is also accepted on the API Keys endpoint (in addition to cookie-based login)

Expanded OAuth Provider Support​

In addition to Google, version 4.0.0 adds OAuth login support for three new providers:

  • Auth0 - enterprise-grade identity management
  • Facebook - social login via Facebook OAuth
  • GitHub - developer-friendly login via GitHub OAuth

All providers are configurable under the new Integrations section.

Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)​

The plugin now integrates with WordPress 2FA plugins. When 2FA is enabled on a user account, the authentication flow enforces the second-factor check before issuing a JWT. This integration is detected automatically at runtime based on the 2FA plugin installed on your site.

JWT Custom Claims​

You can now define custom JWT payload claims directly from the plugin settings. This allows you to embed additional user metadata or application-specific data into every token your site issues, without writing custom code.

Multiple JWT Decryption Keys​

The plugin now supports configuring multiple JWT decryption keys with rules based on the JWT header or payload. This enables key rotation strategies and multi-tenant scenarios where different tokens are signed with different keys.

Refresh Token Handling​

Authentication responses now include a refresh token alongside the access JWT. A dedicated endpoint lets clients exchange an expired access token for a new one using the refresh token, without requiring the user to re-authenticate.

Enable/Disable Revoke and Validate Token Endpoints​

The token revocation and validation endpoints can now be individually toggled on or off from the plugin settings, giving you fine-grained control over which JWT operations are exposed on your site.

WordPress Default Emails on Register and Password Change​

You can now opt in to sending WordPress default notification emails when a user registers via the plugin or changes their password through the reset-password endpoint. Previously this was not configurable and the default WP emails were suppressed.

Try Now Feature​

A new "Try Now" button in the plugin settings lets you test your JWT configuration directly from the admin panel, without needing an external REST client.

OpenAPI Specification​

The old Postman collection has been replaced with a full OpenAPI (Swagger) specification (openapi/openapi.yaml). This provides a standardized, machine-readable API contract that works with any OpenAPI-compatible tooling.

User Identification Moved to General Settings​

The User Identification setting (how the plugin resolves which WordPress user a JWT refers to) has been moved from individual endpoint settings to a single place under General Settings. This eliminates duplication and ensures consistent behavior across all endpoints.

Search on Hooks View​

The hooks/actions reference view now includes a search field, making it easy to find specific action hooks when building integrations.

Bug Fixes​

  • Fix double encoding for Reset Password email body (#165) - the email body was being base64-encoded twice, producing garbled content in some mail clients
  • Fix passwords with special characters on register, authenticate, and reset password - special characters in passwords no longer break authentication due to incorrect wp_slash() handling
  • Replace variables in reset password email subject - template variables (for example, {site_name}) are now correctly substituted in the email subject line, not just the body
  • Fix reset password response - the endpoint now returns a consistent and correctly structured JSON response
  • Fix OAuth + 2FA integration - OAuth login flows now correctly trigger the 2FA check when the authenticated user has 2FA enabled
  • Fix "Try Now" when permalink is disabled - the feature now works correctly on WordPress installations using plain (query string) permalinks
  • Fix WordPress data dependency issue affecting some edge cases in the authentication flow
  • Fix CSS compatibility for WordPress 7.0
  • Fix status codes - HTTP response codes are now accurate and consistent across all endpoints (for example, 401 for unauthorized, 403 for forbidden, 422 for validation errors)
  • Fix validation error responses - invalid request payloads now return structured error messages instead of generic failures
  • Address WordPress Plugin Checker issues - the plugin now passes the official WordPress Plugin Check tool with no critical errors

Breaking Changes​

Version 4.0.0 introduces breaking changes. If you are upgrading from version 3.x, review each item below and update your client applications accordingly.

Settings Structure Reorganized in the Database​

The internal format of the plugin's settings record in the WordPress options table has been restructured. A settings migration runs automatically on plugin activation, but if you have custom code that reads simple_jwt_login_settings directly from the database, update it to match the new structure.

Register User Response Format Changed​

The register endpoint response has changed:

Before (3.x):

{ "success": true, "ID": 1, "user_login": "john", ... }

After (4.0.0):

{ "success": true, "data": { "id": 1, "user_login": "john", ... } }

Update any client code that reads fields directly from the register response root.

Old /register Endpoint Removed​

The legacy GET/POST /simple-jwt-login/v1/register endpoint has been removed.

All user registration must now go through the POST /simple-jwt-login/v1/users route. Update your integrations accordingly.

User Identification Removed from Delete User Settings​

The "User Identification" field has been removed from the Delete User endpoint settings. The plugin now uses the single General Settings > User Identification value for all endpoints.

If you had a different identification strategy configured specifically for delete, review your General Settings to ensure the correct value is set.

Refresh Token Added to Authentication Response​

The authenticate endpoint now returns a refresh_token field in addition to the JWT. While this is additive, clients that strictly validate the response shape (for example, with JSON Schema) may need to be updated to allow the new field.

2FA Enforcement on Authentication​

If your site has a 2FA plugin installed and a user has 2FA enabled, the JWT authentication flow now requires the second factor before issuing a token. Applications that bypassed 2FA by using the plugin's authentication endpoint are now blocked until they implement the 2FA challenge/response flow.

If you encounter any issues after updating, please open an issue on GitHub.

item.title: New Plugin Release 3.6.5
item.description: Simple JWT Login 3.6.5 release notes for the WordPress JWT authentication plugin - security patch, bug fixes, and WordPress 6.9 compatibility.
item.content:encoded:
The version 3.6.5 has been released today on WordPress.

This is a security and maintenance release. Update immediately.

Security Fix​

This release addresses a Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability identified as CVE-2025-58648. Stored XSS vulnerabilities allow an attacker to inject malicious scripts that are persisted on the server and executed in the browsers of other users. This fix prevents unsanitized input from being stored and rendered as HTML.

If you are running an older version, please update as soon as possible to protect your site and users.

  • Fix CVE-2025-58648 - Stored Cross-Site Scripting vulnerability (PR #162)

Bug Fixes​

  • Fix Reset Password: the function was not applying base64 encoding logic, preventing users from using special characters in their passwords (#161, PR #163)
  • Fix PHP session initialization warning (#159)

Compatibility​

  • Update WordPress 6.9 Compatibility

If you encounter any issues after updating, please open an issue on GitHub.
